quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (contractions).
quests.hint: 'I'm', 'they've' and 'it's' are single-beat contractions; 'they've' sounds like 'thave'.
quests.explanation: A contraction glues a pronoun to the verb, so the pair takes one beat instead of two. 'they've' is [ðeɪv], not 'they have'.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm sure they've left; it's already past nine.
quests.phoneticHint: 'I'm' is [aɪm], 'they've' is [ðeɪv], and 'it's' is [ɪts].
commonMistakes: Saying the full forms 'I am', 'they have' and 'it is'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a regretful comment.
quests.hint: 'shouldn't have' sounds like 'shouldn't-uv', with 'have' reduced to [əv].
quests.explanation: In a negative modal plus have, keep 'shouldn't' clear and reduce 'have' to a weak [əv]. 'you're' is [jɔːr] or [jər] in fast speech.
quests.textToSpeak: You're right; we shouldn't have waited so long.
quests.phoneticHint: [jɔːr ˈraɪt], [wi ˈʃʊdnt əv ˈweɪtɪd soʊ ˈlɔːŋ].
commonMistakes: Dropping the [nt] of 'shouldn't', so it sounds like 'should have'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a mild regret.
quests.hint: 'we'd have' and 'they'd' contain a light [d]; 'wouldn't' ends with a quick [nt].
quests.explanation: 'we'd' is [wiːd] and 'we'd have' runs as [wiːd əv]. 'they'd told' contracts 'had'. The cluster in 'wouldn't' needs care.
quests.textToSpeak: We'd have gone earlier if they'd told us it wouldn't take long.
quests.phoneticHint: [wid əv ˈgɒn ˈɜːrliər], [ðeɪd ˈtoʊld], [ˈwʊdnt].
commonMistakes: Saying 'they'd' as 'they would' when it means 'they had'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a rushed reply, using the reductions.
quests.hint: In speech, 'going to' often becomes 'gonna' and 'have to' becomes 'hafta': 'gonna hafta'.
quests.explanation: The reductions squash two words into one quick unit. 'going to' becomes [ˈgʌnə]. 'have to' becomes [ˈhæftə], with the [v] devoiced to [f].
quests.textToSpeak: I'll be late, so I'm going to have to run.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪl bi ˈleɪt], [soʊ aɪm ˈgʌnə ˈhæftə ˈrʌn].
commonMistakes: Saying the full 'going to' with a clear [tuː]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would to a friend.
quests.hint: 'want to' becomes 'wanna', and 'kind of' becomes 'kinda'.
quests.explanation: Both reductions turn the second word into a schwa. The stress stays on 'want', 'eat', 'kind' and 'break'.
quests.textToSpeak: Do you want to get something to eat? I kind of need a break.
quests.phoneticHint: [dʒu ˈwɒnə ˈget ˈsʌmθɪŋ tu ˈiːt], [aɪ ˈkaɪndə ˈniːd ə ˈbreɪk].
commonMistakes: Using both reductions in formal speech

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a reluctant plan.
quests.hint: 'got to' becomes 'gotta', 'ought to' becomes 'oughta', and 'don't want to' becomes 'don't wanna'.
quests.explanation: These forms don't change the meaning, but they change the rhythm: the [t] before 'to' is often tapped and 'to' becomes [ə].
quests.textToSpeak: I've got to call them, and I ought to apologise; I don't want to make it worse.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪv ˈgɒɾə ˈkɔːl əm], [aɪ ˈɔːɾə əˈpɒlədʒaɪz], [aɪ ˈdoʊn ˈwɒnə].
commonMistakes: Pronouncing the [t] in 'got to' as a hard stop
Saying 'apologise' with stress on the first syllable

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (question reductions: 'what are you', 'do you').
quests.hint: 'what are you' sounds like 'whatcha', and 'do you' sounds like 'dyuh'.
quests.explanation: Question openers fuse: [t]+[j] makes [tʃ] in 'what you', and 'do you' becomes [dʒə]. The main verb carries the stress.
quests.textToSpeak: What are you doing later? Where do you want to meet?
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈwɒtʃə ˈduːɪŋ ˈleɪtər], [ˈweərdʒə ˈwɒnə ˈmiːt].
commonMistakes: Saying every word in full: 'what are you'
Making the [tʃ] sound like a separate [t] and [j]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a quick question.
quests.hint: 'how do you' sounds like 'how-dya', and 'why did you' sounds like 'why-dja'.
quests.explanation: 'do you' becomes [dʒə], and 'did you' becomes [dɪdʒə]. The stress moves to 'spell' and 'leave'.
quests.textToSpeak: How do you spell that? And why did you leave so early?
quests.phoneticHint: [haʊ dʒə ˈspel ðæt], [waɪ ˈdɪdʒə ˈliːv].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a casual question.
quests.hint: 'Any idea' links as 'eni-idea', 'when they'll' runs together, and 'Do you have a' shrinks to 'dyuh-hav-a'.
quests.explanation: 'Any idea' has the peak on 'i-DEA', and 'Do you have a' reduces to [dʒə hæv ə]. The stress falls on 'idea', 'back' and 'number'.
quests.textToSpeak: Any idea when they'll be back? Do you have a number?
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈeni aɪˈdɪə wen ðeɪl bi ˈbæk], [dʒə hæv ə ˈnʌmbər].
commonMistakes: Stressing 'do' at the start of the second question

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a phone message.
quests.hint: 'him' and 'her' lose their [h] when unstressed: tell-im, ask-er.
quests.explanation: In pronouns and auxiliaries, [h] is often dropped when the word isn't stressed. The final consonant of the previous word links to the vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: Tell him I called, and ask her to call me back.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈtel ɪm aɪ ˈkɔːld], [ˈæsk ər tə ˈkɔːl mi ˈbæk].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a follow-up question.
quests.hint: 'his', 'her' and 'has' lose their [h] in speech: 'is message', 'to er', 'she 'asn't'.
quests.explanation: The [h] disappears from function words after another word, but not at the start of a sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Have you seen his message? I sent it to her, but she hasn't replied.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈhæv ju ˈsiːn ɪz ˈmesɪdʒ], [aɪ ˈsent ɪt tu ər].
commonMistakes: Dropping the [h] from 'Have' at the start
Stressing 'her' as much as the verbs

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would report a conversation.
quests.hint: 'him', 'he had' and 'he'd have' lose their [h] after other words.
quests.explanation: Only the first content word of each unit keeps its [h]. In 'he'd have a look', the linking makes 'he'd-a-vuh-look'.
quests.textToSpeak: I asked him whether he had time, and he said he'd have a look.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪ ˈæskt ɪm ˈweðər i ˈhæd ˈtaɪm ən i ˈsed id əv ə ˈlʊk].

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (reduced 'and').
quests.hint: 'and' shrinks to 'n' in fixed pairs: fish-'n'-chips, bread-'n'-butter.
quests.explanation: In common pairs, 'and' is reduced to a syllabic [n] or [ən]. The two nouns keep the stress.
quests.textToSpeak: I ordered fish and chips, and my dad wanted bread and butter.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈfɪʃ ən ˈtʃɪps], [ˈbred n ˈbʌtər].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as casual advice.
quests.hint: 'them' often becomes 'em' and 'because' becomes 'cuz'.
quests.explanation: In casual speech, 'them' loses its [ð] and becomes [əm]. 'because' loses its first syllable and becomes [kəz].
quests.textToSpeak: Give them a call; I told them you'd be free, because they asked.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈgɪv əm ə ˈkɔːl], [kəz ðeɪ ˈæskt].
commonMistakes: Saying 'because' with a strong first syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a friendly offer.
quests.hint: 'cup of' becomes 'cuppa', and 'couple of' becomes 'coupla'.
quests.explanation: The 'of' merges into the noun: the [v] disappears and only a schwa remains. The next noun carries the stress.
quests.textToSpeak: I'd love a cup of tea and a couple of biscuits, if you have some.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪd ˈlʌv ə ˈkʌpə ˈtiː ən ə ˈkʌplə ˈbɪskɪts].

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (chunks: 'kind of', 'a lot of', 'out of').
quests.hint: The chunks 'kind of', 'a lot of' and 'out of' run together like single words.
quests.explanation: These chunks stress the noun or adjective after them and reduce 'of' to a schwa. The whole chunk sounds like 'kinda', 'alotta', 'outta'.
quests.textToSpeak: It's kind of cold, and a lot of people are out of town.
quests.phoneticHint: [ɪts ˈkaɪndə ˈkoʊld], [ən ə ˈlɒtə ˈpiːpəl], [ər ˈaʊtə ˈtaʊn].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a weary comment.
quests.hint: 'out of' and 'kind of' run together; 'a lot' finishes the sentence with stress on 'lot'.
quests.explanation: When 'a lot' is at the end of a sentence, it keeps its stress on 'lot'. Chunks in the middle reduce more.
quests.textToSpeak: We're out of sugar again; that's the kind of thing that happens a lot.
quests.phoneticHint: [wɪr ˈaʊtə ˈʃʊgər əˈgen], [ðæts ðə ˈkaɪndə ˈθɪŋ ðət ˈhæpənz ə ˈlɒt].
commonMistakes: Pronouncing 'kind of' and 'out of' with a full vowel and [v]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a story about a day out.
quests.hint: 'lots of' and 'couple of' become 'lotsa' and 'coupla'; 'hours to' links.
quests.explanation: 'to' before a verb is a weak [tə], so 'hours to kill' sounds like 'ow-ers-ta-kill'.
quests.textToSpeak: There were lots of kids, and we had a couple of hours to kill.
quests.phoneticHint: [ðer wər ˈlɒtsə ˈkɪdz], [wi hæd ə ˈkʌplə ˈaʊərz tə ˈkɪl].
commonMistakes: Giving 'to' a full vowel in 'hours to kill'
Saying the [s] of 'lots' with a break before 'of'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a contrast between people.
quests.hint: 'can' is weak in the middle of a sentence, but strong at the end: [kæn].
quests.explanation: At the end of a clause, 'can' has nothing after it, so it gets stress and keeps its full vowel. Weak forms are only for unstressed positions.
quests.textToSpeak: I can, and she can, but I don't think they can.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪ ˈkæn ən ʃi ˈkæn bət aɪ ˈdoʊnt ˈθɪŋk ðeɪ ˈkæn].
commonMistakes: Weakening 'can' when it ends a clause

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as two quick questions.
quests.hint: The last words 'for' and 'at' are strong at the end of the question: [fɔːr], [æt].
quests.explanation: A preposition at the end of a question keeps a full vowel and gets a bit of stress. If more words follow, it reduces to [fər] or [ət].
quests.textToSpeak: Who are you waiting for? What are you looking at?
quests.targetPhoneme: strong forms of prepositions at the end
quests.phoneticHint: [huː ər ju ˈweɪtɪŋ ˈfɔːr], [ˈwɒt ər ju ˈlʊkɪŋ ˈæt].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a puzzled comment.
quests.hint: 'from' is strong at the end of both clauses: [frɒm].
quests.explanation: Compare 'from Spain' [frəm ˈspeɪn], where 'from' is weak, with 'where he's from' [frɒm], where it is strong.
quests.textToSpeak: Where does he come from? I'm not sure where he's from.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈweər dəz i kəm ˈfrɒm], [aɪm ˈnɒt ˈʃʊr weər iz ˈfrɒm].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a warm greeting.
quests.hint: 'how's it going' sounds like 'how-zit-goin', and 'what have you been up to' sounds like 'whatcha-bin-up-ta'.
quests.explanation: Greetings are said as fixed chunks, with the beat on 'how', 'time', 'see', 'been' and 'up'. Everything else shrinks.
quests.textToSpeak: Hey, how's it going? Long time no see; what have you been up to?
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈhaʊzɪt ˈgoʊɪŋ], [ˈwɒtʃə bɪn ˈʌp tə].
commonMistakes: Making 'been' long, as [biːn], in 'what have you been'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a warm goodbye.
quests.hint: 'see you later', 'talk to you' and 'thanks a lot' are said as chunks: see-ya-lay-der, talk-ta-ya, thanks-a-lot.
quests.explanation: Farewells are reduced heavily. 'you' becomes [jə], 'to' becomes [tə], and 'a' links to the next word.
quests.textToSpeak: See you later! Talk to you soon, and thanks a lot for everything.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈsiː jə ˈleɪɾər], [ˈtɔːk tə jə ˈsuːn], [ˈθæŋks ə ˈlɒt].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite request Watch the ritual phrases: polite repair.
quests.hint: 'didn't get that' sounds like 'didn' get that', and 'would you' sounds like 'wouldja'.
quests.explanation: 'would you' fuses to [wʊdʒə]. 'mind repeating it' links in a smooth chain: min-dree-pee-ting-it.
quests.textToSpeak: Excuse me, I didn't get that. Would you mind repeating it?
quests.phoneticHint: [ɪkˈskjuːz mi aɪ ˈdɪdnt ˈget ðæt], [ˈwʊdʒə ˈmaɪnd rɪˈpiːtɪŋ ɪt].
commonMistakes: Saying 'would you' as two full words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a quick chat at work.
quests.hint: 'what do you' becomes 'whaddaya', and 'got to' becomes 'gotta'.
quests.explanation: This speaker uses several reductions in a row. Keep the stress on 'think', 'do', 'know' and 'decide', and squash the rest.
quests.textToSpeak: What do you think we should do about it? I don't know, but we've got to decide soon.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈwɒdəjə ˈθɪŋk wi ʃəd ˈduː əˈbaʊɾɪt], [aɪ ˈdoʊn ˈnoʊ bət wiv ˈgɒɾə dɪˈsaɪd ˈsuːn].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a follow-up question Watch the mixed connected speech.
quests.hint: 'have you had a' runs together, 'talk to him' sounds like 'talk-ta-im', and 'he said he'd' sounds like 'he-said-eed'.
quests.explanation: This is dialogue: several small words reduce while the content words stand out. 'him' loses its [h], and 'to' becomes [tə].
quests.textToSpeak: Have you had a chance to talk to him? He said he'd call you back, but I haven't heard anything.
quests.phoneticHint: [əv jə ˈhæd ə ˈtʃæns tə ˈtɔːk tə ɪm], [i ˈsed id ˈkɔːl jə ˈbæk].
commonMistakes: Splitting 'have you had a' into separate stressed words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an honest confession.
quests.hint: 'was going to' sounds like 'wuz gonna', 'thought you' like 'thaw-chu', and 'slipped my' like 'slipt-my'.
quests.explanation: Notice the [t]+[j] fusion in 'thought you'. The -ed in 'slipped' is a quiet [t]. 'going to' shrinks to [gʌnə].
quests.textToSpeak: I was going to tell you, but I thought you already knew, and then it just slipped my mind.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪ wəz ˈgʌnə ˈtel jə bət aɪ ˈθɔːtʃə ɔːlˈredi ˈnuː].
commonMistakes: Saying 'thought you' with a clear [t] and [j]
Giving 'was' a full vowel and stress, as 'WAHZ'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would on a phone call Watch the phone speech: connected features.
quests.hint: Watch 'it's Nina', 'from the' [frəm ðə], 'calling about' [ˈkɔːlɪŋ əˈbaʊt], and 'asked us' [æskt əs].
quests.explanation: This phone greeting combines contractions, weak forms and linking. Keep the stressed beats on 'Nina', 'clinic', 'calling', 'appointment' and 'move'.
quests.textToSpeak: Hi, it's Nina from the clinic; I'm calling about the appointment you asked us to move.
quests.phoneticHint: [haɪ ɪts ˈniːnə frəm ðə ˈklɪnɪk], [aɪm ˈkɔːlɪŋ əˈbaʊt ði əˈpɔɪntmənt jə ˈæskt əs tə ˈmuːv].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite work message.
quests.hint: 'let me know' runs together, 'can' is weak, 'kind of' becomes 'kinda', and 'short on' links.
quests.explanation: Polite requests use light words; only 'let', 'know', 'make', 'Friday', 'short' and 'time' are strong.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you let me know if you can make it on Friday? We're kind of short on time.
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈkʊdʒə ˈlet mi ˈnoʊ ɪf jə kən ˈmeɪk ɪt ɒn ˈfraɪdeɪ], [wɪr ˈkaɪndə ˈʃɔːrt ɒn ˈtaɪm].
commonMistakes: Saying 'can' with a strong vowel, as [kæn]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a service-desk apology.
quests.hint: 'sorry to' [ˈsɒri tə], 'keep you' [ˈkiːp jə], 'sort out a' [ˈsɔːr ˈtaʊt ə], and 'with you in a' link into chains.
quests.explanation: This is a service-desk apology: reduce the small words and link 'sort out a' and 'with you in a' into smooth chains.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm sorry to keep you waiting; I had to sort out a problem, but I'll be with you in a minute.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪm ˈsɒri tə ˈkiːp jə ˈweɪtɪŋ], [aɪ hæd tə ˈsɔːr ˈtaʊɾə ˈprɒbləm].
